title: Can ChatGPT Pass High School Exams on English Language Comprehension?
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can successfully complete Dutch national high school exams in English reading comprehension, and what that implies for educational assessment. The core question is not whether students learn more with generative AI, but whether large language models can perform at or above the level of secondary students on a high-stakes literacy-related assessment. The author also compares GPT-3.5 with GPT-4 and explores whether repeated querying with stochastic variation can help identify uncertain or potentially incorrect answers.

The study used the three available 2022 Dutch VWO national exams in English reading comprehension, chosen because they postdated ChatGPT’s training cutoff and therefore reduced contamination concerns. GPT-3.5 was first tested through the ChatGPT web interface, with occasional re-prompting when the model failed to provide a valid answer. GPT-4 was then tested through the API in a fully automated workflow without re-prompting. The exams included multiple-choice and open-response items focused on reading comprehension skills such as identifying main ideas, making inferences, and interpreting vocabulary in context. The context is the Netherlands, specifically the academically rigorous VWO high school track.

The main finding is that GPT-3.5 performed roughly at the level of the average Dutch student on these exams, while GPT-4 outperformed the average student. GPT-3.5 obtained a mean grade of 7.3 with re-prompting and 6.5 without it; GPT-4 obtained mean grades of 8.3 and 8.1 for the March and June 2023 versions, respectively. A bootstrapping/self-consistency analysis showed that inconsistent responses were more likely to be wrong, suggesting that output variability can signal uncertainty, though it did not improve final accuracy. The paper concludes that large language models pose clear challenges for the integrity of computer-based literacy assessments and may require educators to rethink assessment design.

The paper does not study a classroom intervention, student learning gains, or durable literacy improvement after AI support. Its conclusions are about AI benchmark performance on high school reading-comprehension exams and the implications for educational assessment. The author also notes an important transferability limit: the exam was English as a foreign language for Dutch-speaking students rather than a native-language English exam, so findings should not be generalized uncritically to other literacy settings.
quality_tier_rationale: Peer-reviewed empirical benchmarking study with clear methods, but it is not an intervention study on students and has no randomization or causal design for educational outcomes. It offers adjacent K-12 evidence about model capability on literacy assessments rather than direct evidence of student learning effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows substantial model performance on literacy assessment tasks, but impact on student outcomes is unclear because no students received a generative AI intervention. Thus educational impact is indirect and not quantifiable as a student effect size.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) was used to answer Dutch national high-school English reading comprehension exam items, benchmarking model performance on K-12 literacy assessment tasks rather than delivering instruction to students.

finding.finding_summary: This study does not measure student literacy learning; instead it benchmarks ChatGPT's performance on Dutch high-school English reading comprehension exams. GPT-3.5 achieved a mean grade of 7.3 with re-prompting and 6.5 without re-prompting, compared with the national student mean of 6.99 on one reported exam cohort (Exam 1 student distribution n=35,698; mean points 35.88, SD=6.48), while GPT-4 achieved mean grades of 8.3 (March 2023) and 8.1 (June 2023). Because outcomes are model exam scores rather than student gains, this is only adjacent evidence for literacy intervention effectiveness.
finding.measure: LLM scores on national high-school English reading comprehension exams; number of correct exam items/points converted to Dutch grades
finding.study_size: 3 exams; 124 total exam questions; student comparison for Exam 1 n=35,698
finding.std_deviation: Student Exam 1 points SD=6.48; item-level subgroup SDs reported for some analyses

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides evidence that ChatGPT can perform at or above average student level on high-stakes K-12 English reading comprehension assessments, implying meaningful implications for assessment integrity and exam design. GPT-4 scored at approximately the 91st-97th percentiles on Exam 1 relative to Dutch student performance distributions, suggesting potential institutional disruption of unsupervised computer-based assessment, though no direct institutional outcome was experimentally measured.
finding.measure: Comparative exam performance relative to national assessment norms and percentile positioning; implications for assessment integrity
finding.study_size: 3 exams; 124 total exam questions; Exam 1 student comparison n=35,698
